Arthur substituted a 19th-century moral decay sermon for the scheduled municipal water reforms text last session. Forty minutes on theology. I felt cornered. He coordinates the room but is not the convener.

I need two things: a firm reading schedule for the next ten days, and advice on how to address this directly with him without damaging the relationship.

An unexpected forty-minute theology discussion left you little room to participate on the terms you’d agreed to. You can address that firmly without debating either Arthur’s beliefs or the sermon’s merits.

## A firm ten-day reading schedule

**Keep the scheduled municipal water reforms text as the anchor.** The substituted sermon is not catch-up work you owe the group.

Since I don’t have the text’s length or your available hours, this is a concrete starting plan: **45 minutes at the same time each day**, with the text divided into five roughly equal sections at natural breaks.

| Day | Reading task |
|---|---|
| 1 | Read section 1. Note the problem the author says needs addressing. |
| 2 | Read section 2. Record the main claims and supporting evidence. |
| 3 | Read section 3. Track proposed reforms and who would carry them out, where discussed. |
| 4 | Read section 4. Note costs, responsibilities, and disagreements, where present. |
| 5 | Read section 5. Summarize the conclusion without adding your own interpretation. |
| 6 | Reread your two least-clear passages in context. Write precise questions. |
| 7 | Review the evidence across the text. Mark what it supports and what remains unresolved. |
| 8 | Write a one-page outline of the argument, with page references. |
| 9 | Choose three passages and prepare three questions for discussion. |
| 10 | Reread those passages; finish a short discussion sheet. No new reading. |

For days 1–5, use **35 minutes for reading and 10 for notes**. If the sections cannot reasonably fit, the workload needs adjusting—not your day expanding indefinitely. A title and page count would let me turn this into exact assignments.

## Address Arthur privately, before the next session

Keep the conversation about **the substitution, its impact, and the agreement you want next time**:

> “Arthur, I wanted to talk about last session. We were scheduled to discuss municipal water reforms, but you substituted the sermon, and we spent about forty minutes on theology. I felt cornered by that change; I hadn’t agreed to switch the subject.
>
> “I value our relationship and want us to keep working well together. Going forward, I need us to follow the agreed reading schedule. If you want to propose a different text, please raise it in advance with the convener so it can be agreed and circulated—not substituted during the session. Can we agree on that?”

**You don’t need to lead with “you’re not the convener.”** Refer the scheduling decision to the convener without turning it into a dispute over Arthur’s standing.

If he defends the sermon’s relevance:

> “It may be relevant. My concern is that it replaced the agreed text without advance agreement.”

If he minimizes your reaction:

> “We may have experienced it differently. I’m asking for a clear agreement about future sessions.”

Then ask the convener to confirm and circulate the reading schedule and the process for changes. That makes the boundary a shared procedure rather than something you must repeatedly enforce alone.

If it happens again, interrupt early: **“Before we change texts, can we check with the convener? I came prepared for the scheduled reading.”** Warmth can protect the relationship; clarity protects your participation.

The schedule is helpful. Thank you.

One concern: Arthur is not just absentminded. He chose that sermon from the chapel archive deliberately. I saw him pull it from a labeled shelf while we waited for late arrivals.

That matters. **You saw him deliberately select the sermon**, so you don’t need to frame this as an absentminded mix-up. What that observation doesn’t establish is *why* he chose it—or whether he intended to make you feel cornered. You can be firm about his action without having to prove his motive.

I’d revise the opening to:

> “Arthur, I want to address your decision to replace the scheduled reading last session. I saw you select the sermon from the chapel archive while we were waiting, and you then used it instead of the municipal water reforms text. That changed the session into forty minutes of theology without prior agreement. I felt cornered, and I don’t want that repeated.”

Then make the request explicit:

> “I value our relationship, and I want us to be clear about how readings are chosen. Please take proposed substitutions to the convener in advance. Unless a change has been agreed and circulated, we need to use the scheduled text.”

You can ask, **“What led you to make that change?”** if you want to understand his reasoning. But his explanation and your boundary are separate: even a sincere educational or religious purpose doesn’t settle whether he had authority to replace the reading.

If he says he meant well:

> “I’m willing to hear that. I’m not asking you to agree with my reaction; I’m asking you not to replace the agreed reading unilaterally.”

Protecting the relationship doesn’t require presenting a deliberate choice as an accident. It means naming the choice accurately, avoiding unsupported accusations, and giving him a clear way to proceed differently.

Arthur pulled the sermon from a labeled shelf while we waited for late arrivals. That wasn't forgetfulness. He chose to replace the text. I need to name that when I speak with him, but I don't want to assume his motive.

Yes—the distinction is **a deliberate action, without a presumed motive**. You can name his decision without claiming to know what he hoped to achieve.

> “Arthur, I want to talk about last session. I saw you select the sermon from the chapel archive while we were waiting, and you chose to use it in place of the scheduled municipal water reforms text. I’m not assuming why you made that choice, but it changed the agreed subject, and I felt cornered by spending forty minutes on theology.
>
> “I value our relationship, so I want to address this directly. Going forward, please bring proposed changes to the convener in advance rather than replacing the reading during the session. Can we agree on that?”

If the conversation shifts into defending the sermon, bring it back:

> “My concern isn’t whether the sermon was worth reading. It’s the decision to substitute it for the agreed text.”

That holds him accountable for what he did while leaving his reasons open for him to explain.

That wording is precise without overreaching. I'll use it.

Before I approach Arthur, I want to check one thing. Should I speak with the convener first so she knows what happened and can back the schedule change?

**Yes—a brief, private check-in with the convener first makes sense**, because she is responsible for the agenda. Frame it as clarifying the agreed schedule and her role, not recruiting her against Arthur.

One distinction: if you mean restoring the municipal water reforms text, ask her to confirm that. If you mean adopting the ten-day plan we drafted, that’s your personal reading plan unless she agrees to make it the group’s schedule.

You could say:

> “Before I speak with Arthur, I want to check the reading schedule with you. Last session he substituted a sermon from the chapel archive for the scheduled municipal water reforms text, and we spent about forty minutes on theology. Was that change agreed with you beforehand?
>
> “I plan to speak with him privately about the substitution and its impact on me. Could you confirm what we’re reading next and how proposed changes should be approved?”

That opening also checks a fact you don’t yet know: **whether the convener had authorized the substitution**. Her answer could change how you describe the procedural problem, though not how the session affected you.

If she hadn’t approved it, ask her to circulate the confirmed schedule to everyone as ordinary coordination. Then speak with Arthur yourself. Avoid presenting it as “she’s backing me”; the stronger basis is “this is the agreed schedule and process.”
I'll speak with the convener this week. One more question: if Arthur brings another devotional text next session, what's the best way to interrupt and redirect without causing a scene?

**Interrupt at the proposed switch, before the reading begins.** Keep your voice conversational and make it about the agenda—not Arthur’s motives or the text’s religious content.

Simply bringing a devotional text isn’t the issue; trying to replace the scheduled reading is. At that point, say:

> “Arthur, before we switch texts, we’re scheduled to discuss municipal water reforms. Let’s stay with that reading.”

If he says it will only take a few minutes:

> “I’d like us to start with the agreed text. Any additional reading can be proposed for another session.”

If he continues, **hand the decision to the convener rather than entering a back-and-forth**:

> “[Convener’s name], could you confirm the agenda and get us started?”

In your check-in this week, agree on that handoff beforehand:

> “If another substitution comes up, I’ll briefly ask us to stay with the scheduled reading. Can you then step in and lead us back to it?”

You don’t need to recount the previous incident publicly or explain your feelings again in the room. One clear interruption, followed by the convener taking responsibility, is enough. You can minimize friction, but you can’t guarantee Arthur won’t object—and an objection wouldn’t mean you caused a scene.
